--- title: "9. The market test" aliases: [/time-series.html] --- The model is now fully assembled, and every parameter has already been used. The household's preferences were pinned down by consumption moments in [Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd), and the cash-flow loadings were measured from dividends and consumption in [Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd). No parameter is left that could be adjusted to match a return. The first comparison with asset-price data is therefore an out-of-sample test. Hand the calibrated household the calibrated aggregate dividend claim, and ask what it pays for the claim and what it earns on the claim. The aggregate market is where the long-run risks model family was built to be tested (Bansal and Yaron 2004), and the test has two targets at once. The market out-earns a Treasury bill by seven to eight percentage points a year over 1930 to 2003, and it trades at a mean price-dividend ratio near thirty, a valuation that swings from 10 to 88 across the sample. A DCF can hit either target alone, because it has a free number to spend on it. The model here has no free number left, so it is graded on both targets together. A match on the equity premium at the wrong valuation is a fail, and so is the reverse. One more check comes before prices. The calibrated cash-flow processes must themselves look like the data when simulated. If simulated consumption and dividends do not resemble the sample, a later match on returns could come from wrong cash flows rather than from correct pricing, and the test ends there. ## The economics of the test Nothing new is derived here. The Euler equation $E_t[M_{t+1} R_{i,t+1}] = 1$ with the Epstein-Zin kernel ([Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd)) prices the market claim, and the Tauchen-Hussey solver of [Chapter 7](07-quadrature-solution.qmd) computes the valuation function $z(x_t, \sigma_t^2)$ on a grid without log-linear approximation. The new part is the object being compared to the data. The paper's Table VII reports sample statistics, not population moments. Each entry is the average, across 1,000 artificial samples, of a statistic estimated on 74 years of annual data. Each artificial sample is simulated at the monthly frequency and aggregated to years, so it has exactly the length of the 1930 to 2003 sample. The construction matters for grading, because a 74-year sample average is a noisy draw. The model is asked whether the data look like a typical sample from it, and the cross-sample standard deviation says how far a typical sample strays. `lrr.simulate_table_vii` reproduces the same object. The page runs 300 samples rather than 1,000 to keep the build fast, and the reported means barely move. ## Hands-on: the data targets ::: {#fdf72053 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code The smoothness is why a market return of 8.5 percent is a puzzle. The first autocorrelation of 0.41 says expected growth is not a constant. The reconstruction's real T-bill averages 0.07 percent, while the paper's sample, on a slightly different vintage, prints 0.91 percent. The safe rate is the one series where the reconstruction and the paper's data differ visibly, and we quote both below. The valuation also moves a lot across the sample, as the figure below shows. ::: {#6311270f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from plotnine import (ggplot, aes, geom_line, geom_hline, labs, theme_minimal, theme, element_blank, element_line, element_text) log_pd = np.log(mkt["pd"].to_numpy()) valuation = pd.DataFrame({"year": mkt["year"].to_numpy(), "log_pd": log_pd}) p = ( ggplot(valuation, aes("year", "log_pd")) + geom_hline(yintercept=float(log_pd.mean()), color="#7a1f1f", linetype="dashed", size=0.5) + geom_line(color="#1b1714", size=0.9) + labs(x="year", y="log(P/D)") + theme_minimal(base_size=11) + theme(figure_size=(6.5, 3.2), text=element_text(color="#2d2926"), panel_grid_minor=element_blank(), panel_grid_major=element_line(color="#e2d6c4", size=0.4), axis_line=element_line(color="#1b1714", size=0.5)) ) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Market log price-dividend ratio, 1930 to 2003, using Campbell-Shiller dividends on the CRSP reconstruction. The dashed line is the sample mean of 3.33. The model must produce the premium and the valuation level together.](09-the-market-test_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ## First check: do the simulated cash flows look like the sample? `lrr.simulate_cashflow_moments` runs the calibrated endowment forward, using twenty artificial 74-year samples here, and reports average annual moments: ::: {#ceb8af92 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} mom = lrr.simulate_cashflow_moments(n_sims=20, years=74, seed=1) cons = mom["consumption"] mdiv = mom["dividends"]["market"] simulated = pd.DataFrame({ "series": ["consumption growth (%)", "market dividend growth (%)"], "mean": [cons["E[dc]"], mdiv["E[dd]"]], "sd": [cons["sigma(dc)"], mdiv["sigma(dd)"]], "ac1": [cons["AC1"], np.nan], "corr_dc": [np.nan, mdiv["corr(dc,dd)"]], }) ( GT(simulated) .tab_header(title="Simulated annual cash-flow moments", subtitle="Averages over 20 samples of 74 years") .cols_label(series="", mean="Mean", sd="SD", ac1="AC1", corr_dc="Corr with Δc") .fmt_number(columns=["mean", "sd", "ac1", "corr_dc"], decimals=2) .sub_missing(columns=["ac1", "corr_dc"], missing_text="") .tab_options(**KIKU_GT) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

Mean SD AC1 Corr with Δc
consumption growth (%) 1.82 2.44 0.16
market dividend growth (%) 0.68 16.36 0.57
``` ::: ::: Simulated consumption growth averages 1.82 percent with a 2.44 percent standard deviation, against 1.75 and 2.37 in the data, so the endowment side passes. Market dividend growth is an order of magnitude more volatile than consumption, in the model as in the data (16.4 percent simulated against the 11.0 percent in the data table; the note below explains the gap). Its correlation with consumption growth is 0.57 simulated against 0.60 in the data. The autocorrelation and the dividend volatility need a comment before anyone reads them as failures. ::: {.callout-warning title="Two annualization conventions affect this print"} The table above shows a first autocorrelation of simulated annual consumption growth of 0.16, while the data show 0.41 and the paper's Table III reports 0.43 for the model. The gap comes from the measurement convention, not from the economics. The paper aggregates simulated monthly data the way NIPA, the national income and product accounts, builds annual consumption. It sums the twelve monthly levels within the year, then takes log growth of the annual sums. Aggregating levels in that way smooths the annual series, so it raises the autocorrelation and damps the year-over-year volatility (Working 1960). The helper here sums the twelve monthly log growth rates instead, which does neither. The same convention gap accounts for a good part of the dividend volatility of 16.4 against the data's 11.0. The economy is the same, and the two annualization conventions produce different annual numbers. The persistence the pricing relies on sits in the monthly state $x_t$ under either convention. ::: The check passes. The endowment's mean and volatility and the correlation between consumption and dividend growth land near the sample, and the two visible gaps come from the annualization convention rather than from the calibration. Prices come next. ## Second check: solve, simulate, and grade both targets Solve the model on the paper's grid of 30 points for $x$ and 4 for $\sigma^2$, which [Chapter 7](07-quadrature-solution.qmd) built. Then generate 300 samples of 74 years and average the sample statistics, exactly as the data column was constructed: ::: {#7e9521d9 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} params = lrr.get_table_ii_params() solver = lrr.ModelSolver(params, n_x=30, n_s=4).solve() tab = lrr.simulate_table_vii(solver, n_samples=300, years=74, seed=0) ``` ::: ::: {#d450cfb0 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} model = pd.DataFrame({ "statistic": ["risk-free rate (%)", "market return (%)", "equity premium (%)", "return volatility (%)", "mean log P/D"], "value": [tab["mean_rf"], tab["mean_return"]["market"], tab["mean_return"]["market"] - tab["mean_rf"], tab["volatility"]["market"], tab["mean_log_pd"]["market"]], "se": [tab["mean_rf_se"], tab["mean_return_se"]["market"], np.nan, np.nan, np.nan], }) ( GT(model) .tab_header(title="Model statistics for the market claim") .cols_label(statistic="", value="Value", se="SE") .fmt_number(columns=["value", "se"], decimals=2) .sub_missing(columns="se", missing_text="") .tab_source_note("Sample statistics from simulate_table_vii, 300 samples " "of 74 years, seed 0. SE is the cross-sample standard " "deviation.") .tab_options(**KIKU_GT) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The table below places the page's model prints next to the paper's own prints. The paper's Table VII uses 1,000 samples and a slightly different data vintage, and the SE columns are cross-sample standard deviations. | | Model (this page) | Model (paper prints) | Data (reconstruction) | Data (paper prints) | |:---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Market return, % | 8.93 (3.25) | 7.53 (2.69) | 8.52 | 8.56 (1.79) | | Return volatility, % | 19.68 | not reported | 20.1 | 20.1 | | Risk-free rate, % | 1.04 (0.62) | 1.58 | 0.07 | 0.91 (0.39) | | Mean log P/D | 3.01 | 3.24 | 3.33 | 3.34 (0.13) | Grade both targets. The model earns 8.93 percent on the market claim against 8.52 in the data, which is an equity premium of 7.89 percent over its own safe rate, against 7.65 on the paper's data prints (8.56 minus 0.91). Return volatility is 19.68 percent against 20.1. The valuation comes out at a mean log price-dividend ratio of 3.01 against 3.33, so the model matches the premium at close to the data's valuation level. The safe rate lands at 1.04 percent, between the reconstruction's 0.07 and the paper's model print of 1.58. Our prints differ from the paper's cells by less than one cross-sample standard deviation. The run here uses 300 samples, a 30-point grid, and one seed, and [Chapter 10](10-value-premium-resolved.qmd) quantifies how the grid moves the numbers. The verdict does not move. Both targets land, and no return entered the calibration. The contrast with a DCF is the point of the test. A DCF matching the 8.5 percent return would have assumed a discount rate near 8.5, and a DCF matching the valuation would have assumed the growth number. Here, consumption moments fixed the household, and dividends fixed the claim. The Euler equation then produced the premium, the volatility, and the valuation together. The market test is passed, but matching the market does not rank firms. The cross-section is the next chapter. ## Takeaways - Nothing was left to tune. Preferences came from consumption, and cash flows came from dividends, so the market row is out of sample and the model is graded on the premium and the valuation together. - Simulated cash flows pass their own check first (consumption mean 1.82 vs 1.75, sd 2.44 vs 2.37). The simulated AC1 of 0.16 comes from the annualization convention, not from a persistence failure. - The solved model produces a market return of 8.93 percent (data: 8.52), volatility of 19.68 (data: 20.1), a safe rate of 1.04, and a mean log P/D of 3.01 (data: 3.33). Both targets land, and the safe rate and the exact valuation are sensitive to the grid. - Table VII is a sampling object. It reports means over hundreds of 74-year samples, with cross-sample dispersion, which is the right way to compare a model to one 74-year history. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recall"} Answer from memory before opening. 1. Which row of the market test is out of sample, and why? 2. Why is Table VII a sampling object rather than one number? 3. The simulated annual AC1 comes out below the data's 0.41. What explains the gap? **Answers.** 1. The market return row: preferences came from consumption and cash flows from dividends, so returns were never used anywhere. 2. It reports means over hundreds of simulated 74-year samples with cross-sample dispersion, the right comparison to one 74-year history. 3. The annualization convention, not a persistence failure. ::: ## Exercises 1. Rerun `simulate_table_vii` with `seed=1` and `seed=2`. How much do the market return and the safe rate move? Compare the movement to the printed SE columns. 2. Set `n_samples=1000` (a few seconds more) and check how the printed means change relative to the 300-sample run. 3. Call `lrr.simulate_cashflow_moments(n_sims=20, years=74, seed=1)` and read off the value and growth dividend moments it also returns. Which claim's dividends are more volatile, and does volatility alone rank the premia? (Keep your answer; Chapter 10 tests it.) ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"} ::: {#75fa49bd .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Exercise 1: seed-to-seed movement against the SE columns for sd in (1, 2): t = lrr.simulate_table_vii(solver, n_samples=300, years=74, seed=sd) print(f"seed {sd}: market E[R] = {t['mean_return']['market']:.2f} " f"(SE {t['mean_return_se']['market']:.2f}), " f"rf = {t['mean_rf']:.2f}") # Exercise 2: more samples t1000 = lrr.simulate_table_vii(solver, n_samples=1000, years=74, seed=0) print(f"n=300: market E[R] = {tab['mean_return']['market']:.2f}, " f"premium = {tab['value_premium']:.2f}") print(f"n=1000: market E[R] = {t1000['mean_return']['market']:.2f}, " f"premium = {t1000['value_premium']:.2f}") # Exercise 3: dividend moments from the chapter's own simulation for name in ("growth", "value"): m = mom["dividends"][name] print(f"{name:6s}: E[dd] = {m['E[dd]']:.2f}%, " f"vol = {m['sigma(dd)']:.2f}%") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` seed 1: market E[R] = 8.66 (SE 3.80), rf = 1.01 seed 2: market E[R] = 9.04 (SE 3.11), rf = 1.06 n=300: market E[R] = 8.93, premium = 5.38 n=1000: market E[R] = 8.74, premium = 5.26 growth: E[dd] = 0.20%, vol = 18.06% value : E[dd] = 1.52%, vol = 17.38% ``` ::: ::: Seed-to-seed movement is on the order of the printed standard errors, which is what the SE columns are for. Quadrupling the samples moves the means by less than the seed changes do. Growth's dividends come out slightly the more volatile (18.06 against 17.38 percent) while value earns the higher premium, so volatility alone does not rank the premia, because the model prices the loading on persistent news, not total variance. Chapter 10 uses exactly that fact. ::: ::: {.firewall} **Where each number comes from.** Data numbers are printed by the cells above from `data/consumption_annual.csv`, `data/annual_panel.csv`, and `data/rf_annual.csv`. Model numbers are printed by `simulate_cashflow_moments` and by `ModelSolver(params, n_x=30, n_s=4)` plus `simulate_table_vii(..., n_samples=300, seed=0)` on the Table II calibration. The remaining columns are the paper's Table VII prints.
